analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax, starting in 2005.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently repeal the estate tax was introduced by Senator Jon Kyl with no cosponsors and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote or hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made the estate tax repeal in the 2001 tax law permanent and moved it up, so that starting in 2005 no federal estate tax would apply to any inheritance. The 2001 law was set to repeal the tax only in 2010 and then bring it back in 2011; this bill would have ended it for good, four years earlier. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. Only estates above a size threshold owe any estate tax at all, so eliminating it entirely would have gone overwhelmingly to the heirs of the wealthiest families, and the very largest estates would have saved the most. Wealthy families planning multi-generational transfers would also benefit from the permanent end of the generation-skipping transfer tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would permanently repeal the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, effective January 1, 2005, rather than allowing the temporary repeal-and-return schedule written into the 2001 tax law to stand. [S2] [S3]

It would accelerate the repeal by four years: the 2001 law repealed the estate tax only for deaths in 2010, with the tax scheduled to return in 2011, while this bill would have ended it for deaths after December 31, 2004. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Estate tax revenue would have been eliminated starting in 2005, and since the federal government must fund its spending from other sources or borrowing, the cost would be spread across all taxpayers. Taxpayers would also be carrying the cost of a permanent cut rather than the temporary one in the 2001 law, whose sunset was designed to limit its budget impact.

drawbacks.text: The estate tax falls only on the largest estates, so a full repeal transfers money primarily to the heirs of the wealthiest families while removing a source of federal revenue that ordinary taxpayers would have to make up elsewhere. [S2] [S3]
Even supporters of the 2001 law had structured the estate tax repeal to expire after 2010, in part to limit its long-term budget cost; making it permanent would have removed that safeguard. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: very wealthy families would keep large inheritances intact and gain certainty about multigenerational planning. The cost is diffuse: federal revenue is gone and must be replaced by other taxes, more borrowing, or less spending. Most households would pay nothing less in estate taxes because their estates were never large enough to owe the tax. The bill also offered no offset for the lost revenue.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Kyl introduced the bill, it was read twice and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Kyl introduced the Permanent Death Tax Repeal Act of 2003 on January 15, 2003, and gave introductory remarks on the floor. [S1] [S5]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day. [S5]
No further action was taken: the bill received no cosponsors and never left the Finance Committee before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005. [S4] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and ordinary taxpayers came out ahead in the narrow sense that no new revenue loss was enacted. Estates large enough to owe the tax in the mid-2000s continued to pay it under the existing phase-down schedule rather than getting a full early repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; large estates kept paying

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks the day it was introduced.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record beyond the Republican sponsorship.

industries.industry: Heirs to the largest estates and wealthy families
industries.note: Full repeal would have eliminated the only federal tax on very large inheritances, four years earlier than the 2001 law scheduled, with the revenue loss falling on the general taxpayer.

industries.industry: Estate planning and trust professionals (lawyers, advisors)
industries.note: Repealing the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes removes the core tax complexity their planning work addresses.
Estate-tax liquidity products sold to large estates would lose their main purpose under full repeal.
